sense: the head of state of a republic

terms.grammar: noun, third declension, masculine or feminine
terms.comment: Classically one who presides over or guards something: the senate was the state’s custōs, praeses, prōpugnātor (Cic. Sest. 137, Lewis & Short), and under the emperors a praeses governed a province. Morgan–Owens takes it for the president of a nation from twentieth-century Latin (Perugini, Egger), with praeses dēsignātus, the president-elect, and praesidis vicārius, the vice-president. The Roman republic had no president: its highest office was held by two consuls (see office, a public office).

evidence: Traupman 180; vice praesidēns, vice president, Traupman 181
terms.comment: Traupman’s other word: the present participle of praesideō, “preside”, used as a noun.

evidence: M-O s.v. president: head of state
terms.comment: Classically prīnceps cīvitātis was a leading statesman, and prīnceps became the emperor’s title (see leader).

terms.gloss: the one at the head of the state
evidence: Cic. Off. 1.85: quī reī pūblicae praefutūrī sunt
terms.comment: A classical way round the title: praeesse, be at the head of, with the dative.

evidence: Cic. Rep. 2.52: rēctor et gubernātor cīvitātis (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: rēctor is classically a guide or ruler; Cicero speaks of the rēctor reī pūblicae, the statesman who guides the state.

phrases.latin: Omnīnō quī reī pūblicae praefutūrī sunt duo Platōnis praecepta teneant
phrases.english: Those who are to be at the head of the state should keep two rules of Plato’s

sources: Lewis & Short: praeses · Lewis & Short: praesideo · Lewis & Short: princeps · Lewis & Short: praesum
